fb389: Do complementary methods help with feeling cold?
fb390: The evidence is limited. According to a review of 20 trials in Raynaud’s phenomenon, biofeedback does not work; heat-retaining gloves were found helpful in a single trial; and no meaningful benefit could be shown for ginkgo, antioxidants or fatty acids. If you would like to try a method, first make sure the underlying cause has been looked into.
fb391: If you would like to try a complementary method, first make sure the underlying cause has been looked into, and think of the method as an addition to medical treatment, not a replacement for it.
fb392: Light, a mirror and ice: the 2026 Nobel Prizes
fb394: The medicine prize went to three pioneers of optogenetics, which lets brain cells be switched on and off with light; the chemistry prize to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who showed how to make only one of two mirror-image molecules; and the physics prize to Francis Halzen, who caught cosmic neutrinos in the ice of the South Pole.
fb395: All three began with a curiosity that looked useless at the time: a pond alga, a reaction that did not add up, and a flash of light at the bottom of the ice. I have explained all three in plain language, with animations.

fb398: What to do in the first 72 hours, how to protect the eye, and why the face should not be forced. When to start exercises, the evidence on acupuncture and electrical stimulation, and six safe things to do.
fb399: In the Cochrane review of nine trials (395 people), acupuncture added to standard treatment of medication and exercise reduced pain by about 30 points out of 100. Acupuncture with a mild electrical current through the needles also reduced pain somewhat compared with a sham treatment; manual acupuncture showed no such difference. The effect lasted about a month and was not maintained at six months. The level of evidence is low to moderate; side effects were mild and short-lived.
fb400: In my own clinical observation, I have seen acupuncture be very effective in fibromyalgia. I share this as my own observation, not as a research finding; not everyone may respond in the same way.
fb401: Deare JC, Zheng Z, Xue CCL, et al. Acupuncture for treating fibromyalgia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013;(5):CD007070.
fb403: According to the Cochrane review of 31 trials (2,257 people), acupuncture may be beneficial after stroke in areas such as independence in daily living, movement, swallowing and pain; no serious side effects were reported.
